titulo: How Rome Really Fell: The Money Behind the Collapse
intro_capitulo: A sausage and a death penalty
descripcion: Rome didn't fall in a day. It took centuries, and it started with a coin. The silver denarius, debased from about 98% silver to about 2%; the Crisis of the Third Century, with at least 26 claimants to the throne in about 50 years; Diocletian's price controls, punishable by death; Constantine's gold solidus; and the final collapse of the West, from Adrianople to 476. First episode of the series: How Empires Fall.
fuentes: Edict on Maximum Prices (301 AD): maximum prices for over 1,000 goods and services, death penalty, patchily enforced, mostly ignored by 305: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_on_Maximum_Prices

Denarius silver content by period (95-98% under the late Republic/Augustus era, 93.5% under Nero, 83.5% c. 148-161, cut from 78.5% to 50% by the Severans, antoninianus later about 2% fine): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarius

Crisis of the Third Century (235-284/285, at least 26 claimants, Plague of Cyprian 249-262, Valerian captured in 260, Gallic Empire 260-274, Severans doubled legionary base pay): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century
Solidus (introduced for mass circulation by Constantine around 312, 72 to the Roman pound, about 4.5 g of gold, stable for about seven centuries): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidus_(coin)

Fall of the Western Roman Empire (Adrianople 378, division of 395, sack of 410, 476, causes cited by historians, Diocletian's army of about 390,000 plus 45,000 in the fleets): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire
Vandal Kingdom: capture of Carthage in 439; North Africa as a major source of revenue and grain for Rome; sack of Rome in 455: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandal_Kingdom

escenas.texto: In the year three hundred and one, the emperor of Rome made it a crime, punishable by death, to charge too much for a sausage.
It wasn't a joke. It was a law with maximum prices for more than a thousand products and services: beef, wine, shoes, freight, even wages.

visual.label: products and services with a price limit

escenas.texto: How did the richest empire on Earth end up there? The answer isn't one battle or one bad emperor. It's a slow story about money, war and power.
And the fall of Rome took centuries. It started with something you could hold in your hand: a silver coin.
Chapter one. The coin.
Rome's everyday money was the denarius. Soldiers were paid in it, taxes were counted in it, and its value came from the metal inside: silver.
Around the time of Augustus, the denarius was almost pure: about ninety eight percent silver.
Then emperors discovered a trick. Melt the coins, mix in cheaper metal, and mint more coins from the same silver. Nero did it in the year sixty four.
Watch what happens to the silver over the next two centuries.

visual.note: silver content of Rome's main silver coin

escenas.texto: By around the year two seventy, the main silver coin was basically copper with a thin silver wash. About two percent silver.

visual.note: a copper coin with a silver wash

escenas.texto: Why do that? Because the biggest bill in the empire was the army. The Severan emperors made the army about a quarter bigger, and doubled a legionary's base pay.

visual.note: and no new silver to pay for it

escenas.texto: There was no new silver to pay for it. So they paid with weaker coins. It's the ancient version of printing money.
And people noticed. When a coin holds less silver, sellers ask for more coins. Prices go up. Today we call that inflation.
Chapter two. The crisis.
In the year two thirty five, the emperor Severus Alexander was killed by his own soldiers. What came next is called the Crisis of the Third Century.
In about fifty years, at least twenty six men claimed the title of emperor. Many of them were murdered.

visual.label: claimants to the title of emperor

escenas.texto: Think about what that means for money. Every new emperor had to pay the army that put him there. More bonuses, more coins, less silver.
Then came disease. A plague, now called the Plague of Cyprian, swept the empire from around two forty nine to two sixty two. Fewer people meant fewer farmers, fewer soldiers and fewer taxes.
And enemies on every border. In two sixty, the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persians at the Battle of Edessa. A Roman emperor died as a prisoner.

visual.sub: Valerian died a prisoner of Persia

escenas.texto: The empire literally broke into three. In the west, a Gallic Empire ruled Gaul, Britain and for a time Spain. In the east, Palmyra took over. Rome kept the middle.
A tough soldier named Aurelian put it back together by two seventy four. He even built new walls around Rome itself. A year later, he was assassinated.
Chapter three. The fix.
In two eighty four, Diocletian took power. He decided one man could no longer run the empire, so he split the job among four rulers. It's called the Tetrarchy.
He also built a huge state. One ancient writer says his army reached almost three hundred and ninety thousand soldiers, plus over forty five thousand in the fleets.
All of that cost money. And prices kept rising. So in three hundred and one came his famous answer: the Edict on Maximum Prices.
The most expensive item on the list was a pound of purple silk: one hundred and fifty thousand denarii. Charging more, or hoarding goods, could cost you your life.

visual.pre: the priciest item: 1 lb of purple silk
visual.label: denarii (maximum price)

escenas.texto: It didn't work. The edict was enforced unevenly, its limits weren't respected, and within a few years it was mostly ignored.
What actually worked came next. Around three twelve, Constantine put a new gold coin into wide circulation: the solidus. Seventy two coins per Roman pound of gold, about four and a half grams each.
And they didn't touch it. The solidus kept essentially the same weight and purity for about seven centuries.

visual.note: stable money outlasted the empire that made it

escenas.texto: That's the first lesson of this story. Price controls fight the symptom. Stable money fixes the cause.
Chapter four. The end in the West.
In three seventy eight, at Adrianople, the Goths destroyed an eastern Roman army. The emperor Valens died on the battlefield.
In three ninety five, the empire was split between two brothers for good: one emperor in the West, one in the East.
In four ten, Alaric and the Visigoths took Rome by starving it, and sacked it for three days. No enemy had taken the city in about eight hundred years.

visual.label: years since an enemy last took the city

escenas.texto: But the deadliest blow wasn't in Rome. It was in Africa. In four thirty nine, the Vandals took Carthage. North Africa was one of the West's main sources of tax money, and of grain to feed Italy.

visual.sub: the West loses its richest provinces

escenas.texto: No taxes, no army. No army, no empire. In four fifty five, the Vandals sailed across and sacked Rome again.
And in four seventy six, a Germanic general called Odoacer removed the last emperor in the West, a teenager named Romulus Augustulus, and the imperial regalia were sent to Constantinople.

visual.titulo: THE LAST CENTURY OF THE WEST

escenas.texto: But here's the twist. The Roman Empire in the East kept going for almost another thousand years, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in fourteen fifty three. And it kept the gold solidus.

visual.pre: the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until

escenas.texto: Chapter five. The pattern.

visual.sub: why empires run out of time

escenas.texto: Historians still argue about why Rome fell, and they list many causes: the army, disease, the economy, bad emperors, civil wars, the administration, invasions, even climate change.
But look at how they connect. Wars cost money. Money gets printed. Prices rise. The army goes unpaid, soldiers pick a new emperor, and the cycle starts again.
Empires rarely fall in a single day. They spend more than they have, they weaken their money to cover it, and they run out of time.

visual.sub: long before they run out of soldiers

escenas.texto: This was the first episode of How Empires Fall. Next: the Spanish Empire, which had the silver of a whole continent, and still went bankrupt. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
